prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a layered aisle layout: shelving stays close along the left foreground (about 0.3–1.5 m), while the open floor, rear wall, and refrigerators extend several metres ahead (roughly 3–8 m). Across frames 1–3, the wearer moves forward and turns right around the end of the shelving, causing nearby shelf edges and products to shift leftward and partly leave view; frames 4–5 reveal more of the open area. In the final frame, the person ahead-right is approximately 1–2 m away, nearer than the refrigerators behind them, while the shelf-end display lies between the wearer and the more distant room. This map makes near/far layering and occlusion boundaries clearer than RGB, but its soft edges, black missing regions, and inconsistent brightness on shelves and the person make metric distances and separations unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map spatially separates several small bottles on the left shelving in frames 1–3, large shelf or display regions near the centre, and, in the last two frames, a person ahead-right plus objects labelled bottle, chair, and TV around the shelf end. It shows that the bottles remain clustered roughly 0.5–2 m from the wearer while the person appears later about 1–2 m ahead-right, with the refrigerator wall several metres behind; the person is partly cut off by the right image boundary and is partially occluded by foreground merchandise. The person’s back is toward the camera wearer, so they face generally away and do not appear to look toward the wearer. The masks make object extents and overlap easier to distinguish than RGB, but many labels are implausible—such as dog, chair, TV, cellphone, and refrigerator assignments—and large shelf regions are merged, so object identity, exact inter-object distance, and arm’s-reach judgments are unreliable.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects no usable body or hand structure in frames 1–4 and only a few yellow body landmarks in frame 5, positioned ahead-right where the RGB shows the other person. Those final landmarks suggest the visible person is about 1–2 m away, facing mostly away from the camera wearer, with an arm extending laterally; no reliable head orientation or gaze direction is recovered. The detected arm appears within the person’s own reach of the adjacent shelf or display, but the map does not establish that the person or surrounding objects are within the wearer’s arm’s reach. Pose could reveal articulated orientation that RGB clothing and occlusion obscure, but here it is highly unreliable because nearly the entire skeleton, both hands, and all earlier motion are missing, while the person is partly outside the right edge.
